First WHU training pilot: Random versus ImageNet initialization¶

Summary¶

This paired pilot asks whether the fixed RID training recipe can learn the WHU Aerial building-footprint target and whether an ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet-B0 encoder improves validation performance over fresh random initialization. Both models use the same saved 100-image training subset, data order, D4 transformations, decoder initialization, optimization rule and 1,036-image provider validation role. ImageNet improves the selected mean per-image validation IoU by 0.098 in this single comparison and produces fewer false building predictions on empty reference images.

This is a validation result from one training subset. It is evidence that the pipeline functions on WHU and that pretraining helps in this pilot; it is not a confirmed external replication, an independent test result or a general geographic-generalization estimate.

1. Research question and evaluation contract¶

WHU differs materially from RID: it provides native 512 × 512 RGB tiles and rasterized building-footprint labels, with label 0 denoting building and label 1 background. There is no separate invalid code. Absolute WHU and RID scores are therefore not directly comparable.

The primary metric is the equally weighted mean per-image building IoU at probability threshold 0.5. For an empty reference and empty prediction, IoU and Dice equal one; any predicted building pixel makes both zero. We retain all 299 empty validation masks in the primary mean. Complementary results report IoU, Dice and pixel average precision (AP) on the 737 positive-reference images and false-building behavior on the empty-reference group. Groups are defined only from reference masks.

from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import Image, display

ROOT = Path.cwd()
RESULTS = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "reports/whu_training_pilot_results.csv")
EXAMPLES = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "reports/whu_training_pilot_examples.csv")

2. Fixed paired method¶

Both EfficientNet-B0 U-Nets start freshly. The ImageNet condition loads only the original verified torchvision encoder weights; both decoders are newly initialized from the same model seed. Training uses ImageNet normalization, joint D4 image/target transformations, the equal-weight BCE and soft-Dice objective, AdamW with weight decay 1e-4, batch size 4 and ordinary BatchNorm updates. The learning rate is 1e-3 through update 2,000 and 1e-4 through update 4,000. Validation occurs at update 0 and every 100 updates. The checkpoint with the highest primary validation IoU is selected, with the earlier update winning an exact tie and update 0 excluded.

The provider test role is absent from training, checkpoint selection and qualitative analysis. The provider documents separate source areas, but the prepared TIFFs lack coordinates needed to reconstruct and independently verify every tile footprint.

method = pd.DataFrame({
    "Training images": [100, 100], "Subset seed": [17, 17],
    "Initialization": ["Random", "ImageNet encoder"],
    "Updates": [4000, 4000], "Validation images": [1036, 1036],
})
method
Training images Subset seed Initialization Updates Validation images
0 100 17 Random 4000 1036
1 100 17 ImageNet encoder 4000 1036

3. Learning trajectories¶

The complete saved validation trajectories show faster learning from ImageNet weights. The rate reduction after update 2,000 visibly reduces the large oscillations, especially for Random. It does not remove model-selection variability: the selected steps differ from the final update for both models.

display(Image(filename=ROOT / "reports/figures/07_whu_pilot_learning_curves.png"))

4. Selected-checkpoint results¶

The table combines best and final validation states, selected-checkpoint metrics, matched training evaluation and measured wall-clock time. The training–validation gap compares both splits using the same selected model in evaluation mode.

columns = {
 "initialization":"Initialization", "best_step":"Selected step",
 "best_validation_iou":"Best val IoU", "last_validation_iou":"Final val IoU",
 "last_validation_loss":"Final val loss", "selected_validation_dice":"Selected val Dice",
 "selected_validation_ap_positive":"Positive AP", "selected_training_iou":"Train IoU",
 "training_validation_iou_gap":"Train–val IoU gap", "total_seconds":"Total minutes"}
summary = RESULTS[list(columns)].rename(columns=columns).copy()
summary["Initialization"] = summary["Initialization"].map({"random":"Random", "imagenet":"ImageNet"})
summary["Total minutes"] /= 60
summary.round(4)
Initialization Selected step Best val IoU Final val IoU Final val loss Selected val Dice Positive AP Train IoU Train–val IoU gap Total minutes
0 ImageNet 3100 0.8099 0.7932 0.2225 0.8553 0.9341 0.9107 0.1008 38.1439
1 Random 3400 0.7116 0.7020 0.2655 0.7705 0.8909 0.8422 0.1306 38.0923

ImageNet raises selected validation IoU from 0.7116 to 0.8099, a paired difference of +0.0983. Its selected validation Dice and positive-image AP are also higher. The final-update difference is +0.0912 IoU, so the conclusion is not created only by checkpoint selection. ImageNet also has the smaller train–validation IoU gap (0.101 versus 0.131).

Optimization took 21.1 minutes per model. Including all scheduled validation and final selected-checkpoint evaluation, each run took about 38.1 minutes on MPS.

5. Positive and empty reference images¶

The primary metric can hide different behavior because an empty mask receives IoU one only when no building pixel is predicted. The table separates groups using the reference masks without changing the primary score.

columns = {
 "initialization":"Initialization", "positive_image_count":"Positive n",
 "positive_mean_iou":"Positive IoU", "positive_mean_dice":"Positive Dice",
 "selected_validation_ap_positive":"Positive AP", "empty_image_count":"Empty n",
 "empty_mean_predicted_building_fraction":"Mean predicted fraction on empty",
 "empty_fraction_with_any_prediction":"Empty images with any prediction"}
groups = RESULTS[list(columns)].rename(columns=columns).copy()
groups["Initialization"] = groups["Initialization"].map({"random":"Random", "imagenet":"ImageNet"})
groups.round(4)
Initialization Positive n Positive IoU Positive Dice Positive AP Empty n Mean predicted fraction on empty Empty images with any prediction
0 ImageNet 737 0.8115 0.8753 0.9341 299 0.0005 0.194
1 Random 737 0.7208 0.8035 0.8909 299 0.0153 0.311

On the 737 positive-reference images, ImageNet improves mean IoU by 0.0906 and Dice by 0.0718. On the 299 empty images, its mean predicted building fraction is 0.049% compared with 1.534% for Random. At least one building pixel is predicted on 19.4% versus 31.1% of empty images. Thus the primary advantage combines better positive-mask overlap with fewer false positives on empty scenes.

6. Common qualitative cases¶

Examples are chosen automatically and identically for both models. Among positive references, paired mean IoU selects one highest-scoring success and one lowest-scoring failure. Among empty references, paired mean predicted building fraction selects one success and one failure. This symmetric rule exposes both models to the same cases and does not access provider-test imagery.

Green denotes true-positive building pixels, orange false positives and blue false negatives.

EXAMPLES

2 empty success val/val_10 False 1.000000 0.000000
3 empty failure val/val_158 False 0.500000 0.178183 
display(Image(filename=ROOT / "reports/figures/07_whu_pilot_validation_examples.png"))

The positive success is segmented accurately by both models. Both completely miss the small positive reference in val/val_0, showing that a high mean does not eliminate severe failures. The empty failure is especially informative: Random labels road-like structures as buildings while ImageNet predicts no building pixels. This case is descriptive rather than a separately sampled error benchmark.

7. Conclusion and limitations¶

The existing training rule works on the imported WHU raster data: both conditions learn far beyond their initial state, and ImageNet is better on every reported selected-checkpoint aggregate. The paired +0.098 validation-IoU difference supports continuing the external-replication study with pretraining as a meaningful factor.

The evidence remains narrow. Only one uniform 100-image subset was trained; model, data-order and augmentation seeds were held fixed, so the experiment varies initialization rather than total training randomness. The same provider validation region selected checkpoints and supports interpretation. Provider-area separation is documented but individual footprint overlap cannot be independently checked from these TIFFs. Neither WHU nor RID test data were evaluated. A useful next bounded step is to repeat the paired comparison on additional predeclared WHU training subsets before expanding training sizes.
